# THE OMNIMASTER FULL-STACK PLAYBOOK ### Frontend, backend, and everything that joins them **Cayelaem Jantjies · Engineer's field textbook · Edition 2026** [GitHub cover](../README.md) · [UI/UX development](OMNIMASTER_HUMAN_INTERFACE.md) · [Volume V: Build with me](OMNIMASTER_BUILD_WITH_ME.md) · [Read the full-stack book on the Study Room](https://omnimaster-study-room.cabo-solutions-za.workers.dev/OMNIMASTER_FULLSTACK_PLAYBOOK.md) --- > I don't call myself full-stack because I happen to know a frontend framework and a database. I use it to describe the work of turning a business need into a usable interface, a reliable API, a trustworthy data model, and a system people can operate. My foundation is Statistics and Data Science. Professional work across banking, manufacturing, research, broadcasting, agriculture and social-impact analytics gradually pushed me upstream and downstream: source SQL, data transformations, dashboards, APIs, backend services, React interfaces, testing, security and cloud delivery. I grew curious about **why the whole system behaves as it does**, not just which line of code renders the answer. This is a practical introduction to the separation between **frontend**, **backend**, and **full-stack integration**. It is for learners, recruiters and engineering reviewers. The exercises are synthetic and reproducible. They are not claims of production security certification or a transcript of private customer systems. ## Contents 1. [What is actually different?](#1-frontend-vs-backend-vs-full-stack) 2. [Frontend engineering: what people experience](#2-frontend-what-people-experience) 3. [Backend engineering: what the system guarantees](#3-backend-what-the-system-guarantees) 4. [A complete feature: from click to committed state](#4-trace-one-feature-across-the-stack) 5. [The third dimension: data and analytics engineering](#5-why-data-engineering-makes-me-a-different-full-stack-developer) 6. [Applied AI: how frontend and backend responsibilities differ](#6-applied-ai-across-the-stack) 7. [Testing and security: no layer gets a free pass](#7-testing-security-and-operations) 8. [UI/UX is a technical responsibility](#8-designing-for-people) 9. [My projects and the boundaries of my experience](#9-what-my-work-demonstrates) 10. [A study project you can build](#10-build-it-yourself) ## 1. Frontend vs backend vs full-stack Think of a booking, application or reporting workflow. Someone wants to find a record, understand it, change something and receive confirmation. **Frontend engineering** builds the experience: navigation, state, content, accessibility, visuals, charts, input and feedback. The frontend helps people understand and complete the task. **Backend engineering** builds trusted operations: identity, access rights, domain rules, data persistence, transactions, integrations, retries, auditing and failures. The backend ensures the action is *allowed and correctly performed*. **Full-stack engineering** connects them with explicit contracts and tests. It follows the user's intention through HTTP requests, policy checks, database writes and responses, and back to a meaningful interface. | Dimension | Frontend | Backend | Their shared responsibility | |---|---|---|---| | Typical execution | Browser/mobile runtime | Server, worker, container or managed runtime | A clear request/response boundary | | Primary focus | Usability and interaction | Correctness, data integrity and authorisation | Useful, reliable outcome | | Typical tools in my work | React, TypeScript, CSS, charts, browser testing | Node.js/TypeScript, APIs, SQL, PostgreSQL/MySQL, background services | Tests, typed contracts, logs, review | | Owns the visual loading state | Yes | Supplies the real operation state | Never show "complete" before completion | | Owns permissions | Useful navigation hints | **Actual enforcement** | Test denied routes end-to-end | | Owns form validation | Fast, helpful feedback | Authoritative rules | Consistent error contract | | Owns durable writes | No | Transactions and persistence | Idempotent UI-to-server actions | | Owns "real-time" meaning | Show freshness context | Source capture, processing and lag | Honest freshness expectations | | Can be tested independently | Components and browser | Units, HTTP and database | Full workflow / user acceptance | **Key distinction:** hiding the Admin button with CSS is not security. A frontend cannot decide for the server who may access a tenant's private data. ## 2. Frontend: what people experience When I build the frontend, my job is not just to make the interface attractive. I ask whether a person understands what the data says and can complete their goal with reasonable effort. ### What frontend developers actually build - **Information architecture:** page navigation, search, grouping and task prioritisation. - **Components and interaction:** reusable controls, forms, modals, tables, charts, filters and details. - **State management:** idle, loading, validating, queued, successful, partially successful, failed, cancelled and stale. - **API consumption:** data fetching, type-safe response handling, cache invalidation and optimistic updates where safe. - **Responsiveness:** layout and interaction across small phones, tablets and large screens. - **Accessibility:** semantic HTML, labels, contrast, keyboard focus, zoom, reduced motion and assistive technology. - **Performance:** fast first interaction, efficient rendering, small bundles and measured bottlenecks. - **Error recovery:** preserve useful input, explain errors and avoid confusing repeated submissions. - **Design quality:** hierarchy, consistency, typography and content that respects the user's mental model. ### Example: an import screen A person selects a source, tests credentials, previews data, validates records and synchronises them. These stages are not equivalent. The user should know when an action merely *checks*, when it *prepares*, and when it changes persistent state. A useful message is **"Preview complete: no records have been published."** A misleading message is **"All done!"** when the server only accepted an asynchronous job. This is why I connect frontend work with UX research. Read [Volume VI: The Human Interface](OMNIMASTER_HUMAN_INTERFACE.md). ### Frontend sketch: model statuses explicitly ~~~tsx type ImportState = | { kind: "idle" } | { kind: "queued"; jobId: string } | { kind: "running"; processed: number } | { kind: "done"; accepted: number; rejected: number } | { kind: "failed"; message: string; safeToRetry: boolean }; function ImportNotice({ state }: { state: ImportState }) { switch (state.kind) { case "queued": return

Queued: {state.jobId}

; case "running": return

Processed {state.processed} rows.

; case "done": return

{state.accepted} imported; {state.rejected} rejected.

; case "failed": return

{state.message} {state.safeToRetry ? "Retry available." : "Check status first."}

; default: return

Choose a source to begin.

; } } ~~~ This illustrates frontend state modelling, not a finished production feature. Actual values must come from the backend, and content needs complete form and accessibility testing. ## 3. Backend: what the system guarantees When I work on the backend, I care about which operations can happen, whose data is involved, what is committed, and what a retry means. ### What backend developers actually build - **API design:** routes, response codes, input schemas, error contracts and versioning. - **Identity:** authentication, sessions, MFA and secure recovery policies. - **Authorisation:** role, operation, tenant and record scope enforced server-side. - **Domain logic:** business rules and valid state transitions, not rules scattered across browsers. - **Database design:** keys, constraints, transactions, indexes, migrations and data consistency. - **Integrations:** SQL sources, APIs, files, webhooks, third-party services and their failures. - **Background work:** job queues, retries, backoff, idempotency and dead-letter handling. - **Operations:** rate limits, observability, secure configuration, recovery and safe rollouts. - **Data governance:** audit trails, retention, provenance and access boundaries. ### HTTP statuses must mean something Imagine a user asks to synchronise data. | Response | Accurate meaning | Interface implication | |---|---|---| | **202 Accepted** | Server accepted work for processing | Show Queued, not Completed | | **200 OK** | The described synchronous operation succeeded | Show the actual result | | **400 Bad Request** | Invalid shape or input | Highlight correctable fields | | **401 Unauthorized** | No valid authentication | Prompt for sign-in safely | | **403 Forbidden** | Authenticated but not permitted | Deny without leaking data | | **409 Conflict** | State/version conflict | Ask user to reload or reconcile | | **429 Too Many Requests** | Request limit reached | Explain safe retry timing | | **5xx** | Unexpected service failure | Report uncertainty; don't assume write didn't happen | ### Backend sketch: enforce policy where it matters ~~~ts // Pseudocode showing responsibilities; not a working Fastify route. async function resolveException(request: RequestContext) { const actor = await authenticate(request); const input = validateResolution(request.body); const access = await authorise(actor, "exceptions.resolve", input.exceptionId); if (!access.allowed) return forbidden(); return db.transaction(async (tx) => { const row = await tx.selectExceptionForUpdate(input.exceptionId, access.tenantId); if (!row) return notFound(); if (row.status === "RESOLVED") return conflict("Already resolved"); await tx.markResolved(row.id, input.reason); await tx.writeAudit(actor.id, "exceptions.resolve", row.id); return success({ status: "RESOLVED" }); }); } ~~~ A transaction protects the combined state change inside the database. Real routes still need schema definitions, secure authentication, tenant lookup, consistent error handling, idempotency and integration tests. ## 4. Trace one feature across the stack ### Case: resolve a fictional delivery exception ~~~mermaid sequenceDiagram actor Person participant UI as React screen participant API as Authenticated API participant DB as PostgreSQL participant Jobs as Background worker Person->>UI: Select Resolve UI->>UI: Validate required reason UI->>API: POST /exceptions/{id}/resolve API->>API: Verify actor + tenant + permission API->>DB: Atomic state and audit update DB-->>API: Commit or conflict API-->>UI: Verified status or safe error UI-->>Person: Explain what actually happened API->>Jobs: Queue post-commit notification Jobs-->>API: Record outcome and retries ~~~ **Frontend responsibility:** make Resolve discoverable, require a meaningful reason, show a submitting state, prevent confusing duplicate clicks and explain success, conflict or unknown outcome. **Backend responsibility:** verify role and tenant, reject stale state, commit the change atomically, record the actor and protect the notification workflow against duplicates. **Full-stack responsibility:** write tests that start from user action and inspect backend truth. A button labelled "Resolved" must never be a substitute for the committed state. ### Common failure: the ambiguous network timeout The browser sends a request. The server commits. The response is lost. The frontend cannot safely assume failure and resubmit. The backend should provide a stable operation identifier or idempotency mechanism, plus a status endpoint. The frontend should say, **"We couldn't confirm the result. Check its status before retrying."** This is where real software engineering differs from demo tutorials. ## 5. Why data engineering makes me a different full-stack developer My foundation is not only frontend and backend code. I have worked with SQL, Power BI, DAX, Fabric-related analytics, ETL/ELT, source integration, modelling and performance across organisations and industries. That experience changes what I ask when building a product: 1. What is the authoritative event, and what does one row represent? 2. Can a join multiply a business amount? 3. How recent is the source, not merely the page render? 4. Can a changed record or delete be missed by an incremental pipeline? 5. Can access rules leak another market's or tenant's information? 6. Are the dashboard's numbers reproducible from source? A product becomes trustworthy when its **data grain, business semantics, API contract and interface wording** agree. ### Learn by building My [Data-to-Decision Platform](../projects/data-to-decision-platform/) demonstrates a synthetic source-event pipeline with versioning, atomic SQLite writes, current-state projection and tenant-specific metrics. It has no external identity layer or live CDC connection; it is an educational simulation. ## 6. Applied AI across the stack An AI feature is not a magic box attached to a button. Different layers own different risks. | Frontend / UX | Backend / data layer | |---|---| | Explain what the AI can and cannot do | Decide whether this task is permitted for the actor | | Show sources, uncertainty and review status | Retrieve approved source material under tenant/role scope | | Provide edit, reject, retry and human-review paths | Validate schema, source IDs, limits and content safety | | Avoid a confident-looking answer with no evidence | Log bounded decisions, costs, failures and provenance | | Preserve user control | Apply deterministic state transitions; no silent consequential writes | ### An education example A teacher asks AI to suggest feedback on a fictional learner answer. The frontend should make the output recognisable as a suggestion, show the relevant rubric and source and offer a deliberate review action. The backend should verify educator access, retrieve only the permitted learner and rubric, bound provider use, validate scoring constraints and require explicit human approval before an official grade changes. My [Offline AI Output Evaluation Lab](../projects/ai-output-evaluation/) teaches a narrow extractive-evidence contract. It does **not** prove semantic truth, privacy compliance or production-level AI reliability. ## 7. Testing, security and operations A meaningful "done" depends on the layer. | Test class | Frontend evidence | Backend evidence | End-to-end question | |---|---|---|---| | Unit | Correct component state | Business-rule invariant | Are the parts internally coherent? | | Integration | Correct API decoding | Actual database operation | Did they agree on schema and semantics? | | Browser | User completes the task | Role/tenant denial is enforced | Does the user journey work? | | Accessibility | Focus, labels, reflow, screen reader | Useful error information | Can different people understand and recover? | | Security | No secrets or false trust assumptions | Auth, MFA, IDOR, input, SSRF and least privilege | Does an attacker bypass the intended boundary? | | Reliability | Honest queued/failed states | Retry, checkpoint, rollback and alerting | What happens when a dependency fails? | | Release | UI assets on intended version | Migration and config on intended version | Did this exact commit pass the right gates? | A green unit suite is useful, but it does not prove a real deploy, accessibility compliance or authorisation on every route. ## 8. Designing for people is engineering UI/UX development matters because a system's job is not just to compute the right output. It must help people *use* the output. The questions I now ask about an interface are practical: can someone find the task, understand the meaning, tell whether something saved, recover when it fails, use the screen on a phone and know what happens to their information? One lesson arrived directly from this portfolio: the "Interactive Study Room" link initially opened an **HTML source file in GitHub** instead of the actual experience. The code was there, but the person could not use it. Fixing the destination was a usability improvement, not a CSS improvement. [Volume VI: The Human Interface](OMNIMASTER_HUMAN_INTERFACE.md) contains full chapters on task design, accessibility, design systems, user research and practical UX exercises. ## 9. What my work demonstrates | Workstream | Frontend or UX work | Backend / data work | Status boundary | |---|---|---|---| | Enterprise BI engagements | Dashboards, reporting UX, semantic labels and visual performance | SQL modelling, transformations, metric definitions and data reconciliation | Historical professional work, proprietary source | | The Fixer / NewChanges | Source previews, admin workflows, responsive/dashboard interfaces | TypeScript/Fastify APIs, PostgreSQL, imports, auth/MFA workstreams, tests | Public code with active gates; not a blanket production-readiness claim | | CABO Learning Hub | Learner, teacher, guardian and admin journeys; assessments and mobile design | Identity, institutional roles, records, AI routing and validation | Active product development; no claimed government rollout | | Financial and HR prototypes | Forms, review flows, reporting and role-aware UX | Transaction rules, auditability, data permissions and domain models | Prototypes/staging with project-specific limitations | | OmniMaster Study Room | Interactive questions, progress, navigation and accessible controls | Hosted delivery and test checks; browser-local progress | Live teaching product; final manual QA remains separate | I am strongest in data engineering, BI/analytics and full-stack application delivery, with growing exposure to cloud/platform operations, security engineering, mobile and AI. **My ability to contribute across much of software-oriented IT is not a claim to be an expert in every specialist niche. Hardware engineering and physical device repair are not my area of focus.** ## 10. Build it yourself: the exception tracker Create a fictional two-tenant exception workflow. Build only one complete path first. **Step A: define the data.** One exception has a stable ID, tenant, status, assigned actor, created timestamp and resolution history. **Step B: design the frontend.** A list, detail page and Resolve action with loading, confirmation, conflict and error states. Test keyboard navigation and a narrow mobile viewport. **Step C: design the backend.** Use an authenticated API, role/tenant checks, valid state transitions, transaction/audit consistency, and an idempotency strategy. **Step D: prove denial.** Try a wrong-tenant ID, a revoked session and a duplicate resolution attempt. Verify no unauthorised state change or leakage. **Step E: make failure understandable.** Disconnect the browser after request submission. Does the frontend promise a retry it cannot justify? Does the backend expose enough state to reconcile what happened? **Step F: document the boundary.** Write a README saying what was implemented, what was tested and what is missing before real deployment. ### Five review questions 1. What must happen on the server even if the browser lies? 2. How does a frontend distinguish "queued" from "done"? 3. Why does a transaction matter for state change plus audit? 4. What happens to the user if a request commits but the response disappears? 5. Which tests prove a feature, and which merely prove a toy component? **The most interesting full-stack skill is not knowing every syntax rule. It is knowing which part of the system owns the truth, how the layers cooperate and what a real person experiences when something goes wrong.** --- **Explore further:** [The OmniMaster Academy](OMNIMASTER_ACADEMY.md) · [Engineering Field Guide](OMNIMASTER_FIELD_GUIDE.md) · [Build With Me](OMNIMASTER_BUILD_WITH_ME.md) · [UI/UX Development](OMNIMASTER_HUMAN_INTERFACE.md) · [Interactive Study Room](https://omnimaster-study-room.cabo-solutions-za.workers.dev/) *Educational text written as a first-person field guide. Examples are synthetic. Private client information is intentionally excluded.*

# THE OMNIMASTER HANDBOOK
## A technical autobiography told through systems, failures, decisions and working code

**Cayelaem Jantjies | Data Engineering · Analytics · Full-Stack Development · Applied AI · Platform Engineering**  
**Edition 01 | 9 November 2026 | Johannesburg, South Africa**

[Back to my GitHub cover](../README.md) · [Interactive portfolio](https://omnimaster-portfolio.onrender.com) · [Professional project atlas](PROJECT_PORTFOLIO.md)

---

> I started with statistics and reports. The questions grew: Where did that number come from? Why did the pipeline fail? Who is authorised to see it? What happens when the database changes while somebody is using the application? Eventually the answer could not fit inside a dashboard. It had to become a system.

This handbook is the long-form companion to my GitHub profile. It is not a generic tech stack dump, a collection of AI-written product claims or a claim to have mastered every platform. Think of it as an open engineering notebook about **who I am, what I have built, how I think, what has gone wrong, how I investigate it, and where I want to go**.

**Continue to [Volume II: The OmniMaster Field Guide](OMNIMASTER_FIELD_GUIDE.md)** for architecture diagrams, debugging casebooks, worked engineering exercises, a role-to-evidence navigator and six decision records. Volume I is the narrative; Volume II is the engineer's desk.

**Study or meet the human:** [Volume III · OmniMaster Academy](OMNIMASTER_ACADEMY.md) teaches the skills with exercises and capstones.

**Learn how I design for people:** [Volume VI · The Human Interface](OMNIMASTER_HUMAN_INTERFACE.md) covers UI/UX development, usability, inclusive interface systems and real product design trade-offs.

**Build a real teaching project:** [Volume V · Build a System With Me](OMNIMASTER_BUILD_WITH_ME.md) teaches a complete synthetic data-to-decision system, with replay, rollback, reconciliation and tests. The [30-day expedition](THIRTY_DAY_ENGINEERING_EXPEDITION.md) turns those skills into daily practice.
 [Volume IV · The Person Behind the Code](OMNIMASTER_OPERATING_MANUAL.md) explains my self-described INTJ habits, systems mindset, collaboration style and IT range. [The Arcade](OMNIMASTER_ARCADE.md) adds executable detective scenarios.

## The four boundaries of my engineering work

~~~mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Understand the source"] --> B["Engineer reliable data"]
    B --> C["Deliver useful decisions"]
    C --> D["Operate and protect"]
    D -->|"feedback, incidents and learning"| A
~~~

A query is not finished because it returns rows. A dashboard is not finished because it has a colour palette. An API is not finished because it returns 200. A model is not finished because its answer sounds plausible. I focus on the boundary **between correct code and useful, trustworthy software**.

## How to read the evidence

Every project or statement should be read with its delivery status:

| Label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Professional delivery** | Historical engagement or responsibility described in my CV and professional record; private source code may not be shareable |
| **Public implementation** | Source is visible in a linked repository; this does not automatically mean deployed or secure |
| **Prototype / synthetic demonstration** | Works with fictional data or limited features; no customer production claim |
| **Staging / active development** | Implemented work or candidate release with outstanding verification or rollout gates |
| **Design direction** | Proposed architecture or product outcome, not evidence that it shipped |
| **CV-reported metric** | Outcome from my professional record, not independently rerun in a public benchmark |

The most important rule: **a PR is not a deployed feature, a passing unit test is not a security certification, and a planned public-sector integration is not a government contract**.

### Companion reference library

The chapters add the narrative and reasoning. These deeper references retain source-specific detail:

[Client case studies](CLIENT_CASE_STUDIES.md) · [Technical skills and evidence](TECHNICAL_SKILLS.md) · [Project portfolio atlas](PROJECT_PORTFOLIO.md) · [Architecture playbook](OMNIMASTER_SYSTEM_DESIGN.md) · [Mission dossiers](OMNIMASTER_MISSION_DOSSIERS.md) · [Engineering field notes](ENGINEERING_FIELD_NOTES.md)

**The principle behind everything here: one mind, every layer.** The OmniMaster persona is creative. The engineering history, open issues, experiments and limitations are not.

# THE OMNIMASTER FIELD GUIDE
### Volume II of my living engineering textbook

**Cayelaem Jantjies · Engineering architectures, investigations, working exercises and technical conversations · November 2026**

[← Return to the main handbook](OMNIMASTER_HANDBOOK.md) · [GitHub profile](../README.md) · [Runnable labs](../projects/README.md)

---

> The main handbook explains where I came from and the systems I work on. This volume opens the engine room: the boundaries, choices, breakages and practical questions that shape my approach.

This is a companion to my ten-chapter [OmniMaster Handbook](OMNIMASTER_HANDBOOK.md). Read it as an engineering field manual and an invitation to inspect my thinking.

## Start where your curiosity leads

| Reader | Starting point | What you'll discover |
|---|---|---|
| **Recruiter or hiring manager** | [04 · Role and evidence navigator](field-guide/04_ROLE_AND_EVIDENCE_MAP.md) | My experience, roles I fit, concrete project references and honest limitations |
| **Data engineer / architect** | [01 · Annotated architecture atlas](field-guide/01_ARCHITECTURE_ATLAS.md) | End-to-end boundaries, CDC, semantics, AI and security |
| **Senior engineer / reviewer** | [02 · The debugging casebook](field-guide/02_DEBUGGING_CASEBOOK.md) | Failure symptoms, competing hypotheses, investigations and safe fixes |
| **Interview panel** | [03 · Engineering workbook](field-guide/03_ENGINEERING_WORKBOOK.md) | Worked problem-solving scenarios, tests and discussion prompts |
| **Technical lead** | [05 · Architecture decision journal](field-guide/05_DECISION_JOURNAL.md) | Trade-offs, alternatives, decision criteria and release evidence |

## Volume II chapters

1. [**Architecture atlas:** trace systems from operational truth to user outcome](field-guide/01_ARCHITECTURE_ATLAS.md)
2. [**Debugging casebook:** how I investigate things that break](field-guide/02_DEBUGGING_CASEBOOK.md)
3. [**Engineering workbook:** exercises, answers and reproducible code](field-guide/03_ENGINEERING_WORKBOOK.md)
4. [**Role and evidence map:** a guided tour for a recruiter or technical leader](field-guide/04_ROLE_AND_EVIDENCE_MAP.md)
5. [**Decision journal:** design records and the trade-offs they expose](field-guide/05_DECISION_JOURNAL.md)

## The central system question

~~~mermaid
flowchart LR
    P["People & business problem"] --> S["Source facts & constraints"]
    S --> E["Engineering decision"]
    E --> I["Implementation"]
    I --> V["Evidence & tests"]
    V --> O["Operating outcome"]
    O -->|"new information"| P
~~~

A strong engineer can move around this loop in either direction. From a failed KPI, trace the measure back to source records. From a security flaw, find the trust boundary. From an attractive product proposal, isolate the business event and the operating cost.

I want these materials to show **how I reason**, not invent achievements. Where a client record cannot be published, I use an explicitly hypothetical illustration. Where the public code contains unfinished work, I name the issue or pull request instead of claiming release success.

## Companion volumes and evidence

- **Volume I:** [The OmniMaster Handbook](OMNIMASTER_HANDBOOK.md), the career narrative and ten technical chapters.
- **Volume III:** [The OmniMaster Academy](OMNIMASTER_ACADEMY.md), seven study modules and capstone blueprints.
- **Volume IV:** [The Person Behind the Code](OMNIMASTER_OPERATING_MANUAL.md), INTJ as self-description and my approach to working across IT.
- **Arcade:** [The OmniMaster Arcade](OMNIMASTER_ARCADE.md), learning puzzles and a runnable incident game.
- **Volume V:** [Build a System With Me](OMNIMASTER_BUILD_WITH_ME.md), six guided lessons and a runnable end-to-end synthetic data platform.
- **Volume VI:** [The Human Interface](OMNIMASTER_HUMAN_INTERFACE.md), UI/UX development, accessibility, human research and measurable usability.
- **Daily practice:** [30-Day Engineering Expedition](THIRTY_DAY_ENGINEERING_EXPEDITION.md) and [offline interactive study room](interactive/index.html).
- **Source archive:** [Project portfolio atlas](PROJECT_PORTFOLIO.md) and [real-world mission dossiers](OMNIMASTER_MISSION_DOSSIERS.md).
- **Professional engagements:** [Client case studies](CLIENT_CASE_STUDIES.md), subject to appropriate confidentiality.
- **Code you can run:** [Four synthetic engineering labs](../projects/README.md), with tests and CI.
- **Live engineering issues:** [The Fixer](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges/issues) and [Learning Hub](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/Training-and-Development-Hub/issues), where some work is intentionally not declared complete.

**Evidence standard:** a design diagram is not proof of deployment. A scenario is not a disclosed client incident. A green unit test is not an operational acceptance test. A career metric from my CV is reported history, not a new benchmark.

# THE OMNIMASTER ACADEMY
### Volume III | Learn the engineering habits, build the systems, and explain the decisions

**A practical study guide by Cayelaem Jantjies · November 2026**  
[GitHub cover](../README.md) · [Volume I: My story](OMNIMASTER_HANDBOOK.md) · [Volume II: Field guide](OMNIMASTER_FIELD_GUIDE.md) · [The person behind the code](OMNIMASTER_OPERATING_MANUAL.md)

---

> Don't copy my job titles. Copy the process: understand the business event, reproduce the bug, model the facts, build the workflow, test the boundaries, and explain the trade-offs.

This is the part of my GitHub where I try to make myself *replaceable in the best possible way*: anyone who is curious and willing to practise should be able to follow the same engineering principles. It doesn't promise you my career or turn six weeks of tutorials into a senior engineer. It gives you a route from a blank repository to a defensible project.

**Who it's for:** a student, career-switcher, BI analyst moving toward engineering, software developer learning data, or engineer curious about applied AI and delivery.

**Cost and access:** the main exercises use Python, SQLite, Git and a code editor. They're designed to run locally with synthetic data, without an AWS account, paid AI API or work-owned credentials.

## Pick a route

| Track | Best for | Start |
|---|---|---|
| **New to engineering** | Build foundations one boundary at a time | [01 · Learn how to learn](academy/01_START_HERE.md) |
| **Already working in BI** | Move upstream to SQL, pipelines, contracts and APIs | [02 · The data model](academy/02_SQL_AND_MODELLING.md) |
| **Already building apps** | Make data and access boundaries trustworthy | [04 · Full-stack workflows](academy/04_BUILD_APPLICATIONS.md) |
| **Curious about applied AI** | Add models to workflows without trusting unvalidated output | [05 · Applied AI with guardrails](academy/05_APPLIED_AI.md) |
| **Preparing for senior interviews** | Prove understanding through negative tests and release criteria | [06 · Security and delivery](academy/06_SECURITY_AND_DELIVERY.md) |
| **Want a portfolio piece** | Build and explain an entire system | [07 · Capstones and evidence](academy/07_CAPSTONES.md) |

## The seven modules

1. [**01. Think like an investigator:** define the problem, tools and learning journal](academy/01_START_HERE.md)
2. [**02. SQL and modelling:** business grain, joins, measures, indexing and tests](academy/02_SQL_AND_MODELLING.md)
3. [**03. Reliable data movement:** ingestion, quality, CDC, retries and history](academy/03_PIPELINES_AND_CDC.md)
4. [**04. Full-stack engineering:** APIs, state transitions, tenant scope and UI](academy/04_BUILD_APPLICATIONS.md)
5. [**05. Applied AI responsibly:** evidence, evaluation, costs and human review](academy/05_APPLIED_AI.md)
6. [**06. Security, testing and release:** negative paths, CI and rollback](academy/06_SECURITY_AND_DELIVERY.md)
7. [**07. Capstones:** combine the layers into a real portfolio narrative](academy/07_CAPSTONES.md)

## A suggested 12-week route

| Weeks | Focus | Minimum evidence you should produce |
|---|---|---|
| 1–2 | Tools, data grain, SQL and modelling | A reproducible source table, schema, query tests and explanation |
| 3–4 | Ingestion, contracts, state changes and replay | Synthetic ETL/CDC simulation, duplicate/deletion tests and failure diary |
| 5–6 | API + database + minimal interface | Authenticated CRUD-style workflow, tests, schema and clear error behaviour |
| 7–8 | Applied AI and risk assessment | Offline evaluator, test cases, human-review logic and explicit no-model fallback |
| 9–10 | CI, secrets, release rehearsal | Automated tests, negative cases, restore/rollback document |
| 11–12 | One capstone and evidence-led communication | README, architecture diagram, demo steps, trade-offs, what failed, what's next |

This is a **suggested study cadence**, not a promise of completion or a qualification. Repeat any module until you can explain it without copying an answer.

## How to measure learning

Use **evidence**, not hours of videos watched. At the end of a module, ask:

1. Can I reproduce the behaviour from clean inputs?
2. Can I explain why the design has this grain and these boundaries?
3. Which failure case did I intentionally create?
4. Can a stranger run the test without my machine or credentials?
5. What remains unproved, and how would I verify it in production?

Write one short engineering journal entry after each module: **problem → hypothesis → experiment → result → decision → remaining risk**.

## Practice repository

Start with the four [public engineering labs](../projects/README.md). They include a CDC replay, data quality contracts, SQL query plans and a synthetic source-grounding evaluator. Next, play the [OmniMaster Incident Academy game](../projects/omnimaster-incident-academy/) to practise reasoning about failure modes.

For worked explanations and reviewer questions, use the [Volume II workbook](field-guide/03_ENGINEERING_WORKBOOK.md). For the story behind these habits, read [Why I work this way](personal/02_WHY_I_THINK_IN_SYSTEMS.md).

## The rules of this classroom

- Never paste employer data, production secrets or real learner/customer records into a tutorial.
- Do not present a lab as a production CDC service, live AI system or security certification.
- Prefer a boring correct solution to an impressive untestable one.
- Record what you couldn't solve. That is how a useful engineering notebook starts.
- Learning a language is not the same thing as understanding its underlying system.

**Graduation means you have a project that another engineer can question, run and improve.** There is no imaginary certificate. Your source, tests and explanations are the credential.

## Go beyond the course

[**Volume V: Build a System With Me**](OMNIMASTER_BUILD_WITH_ME.md) supplies a complete fictional SQLite pipeline with six guided engineering chapters, replay and failure tests. [The 30-day expedition](THIRTY_DAY_ENGINEERING_EXPEDITION.md) turns the syllabus into daily artifacts. For a more playful format, open the [live interactive Study Room](https://omnimaster-study-room.cabo-solutions-za.workers.dev/) in any browser.


[Start lesson 01 →](academy/01_START_HERE.md) · [Try the arcade →](OMNIMASTER_ARCADE.md)


**Design for people:** [Volume VI](OMNIMASTER_HUMAN_INTERFACE.md) adds a six-chapter UI/UX development and usability course.


### Read lessons without opening GitHub

The [live OmniMaster Study Room](https://omnimaster-study-room.cabo-solutions-za.workers.dev/) serves all Academy lessons directly as readable HTML. The [frontend/backend book](https://omnimaster-study-room.cabo-solutions-za.workers.dev/OMNIMASTER_FULLSTACK_PLAYBOOK.md) and its [PDF edition](https://omnimaster-study-room.cabo-solutions-za.workers.dev/downloads/omnimaster-fullstack.pdf) are part of the same public learning experience.

# THE PERSON BEHIND THE CODE
### Volume IV | My operating manual: INTJ, curiosity, independence and building across IT

**Cayelaem Jantjies | A first-person explanation of how I work, not a personality verdict**

[← GitHub cover](../README.md) · [Volume I: Career story](OMNIMASTER_HANDBOOK.md) · [Volume III: Learn my methods](OMNIMASTER_ACADEMY.md) · [Have some fun](OMNIMASTER_ARCADE.md)

---

> If you give me a dashboard problem, I want to inspect the source SQL. If the SQL depends on a broken data flow, I want to inspect the pipeline. If the pipeline depends on a fragile API or permissions model, I will go there too. I don't follow the org chart when debugging. I follow the system.

## The core statement

**I can probably contribute almost anywhere across the software-facing side of IT. Hardware engineering and physical device repair are not my lane.**

That is a statement about **breadth, problem-solving range and adaptability**, not a claim that I am already an expert in every niche or qualified for every specialist role. My strongest evidence is in **data engineering, BI/analytics, full-stack application development and cross-layer delivery**. My growing areas include platform architecture, DevSecOps, cloud systems, applied AI and native mobile work. Fields such as specialist offensive security, deep network engineering, kernel development or regulated infrastructure operations require their own experience and verification.

I have worked across enough industry and technology boundaries to know that learning a new tool is often easier than untangling an unclear business process.

## The chapters

| Chapter | Read this to understand |
|---|---|
| [01 · INTJ: the label and the lived habits](personal/01_INTJ_AND_ME.md) | My self-described personality pattern, strengths, blind spots and why personality labels have limits |
| [02 · Why I think in systems](personal/02_WHY_I_THINK_IN_SYSTEMS.md) | The influence of statistics, BI, debugging and product ownership on my thinking |
| [03 · Where I fit across IT](personal/03_IT_RANGE_AND_LIMITS.md) | My technical breadth, strongest proof and honest ramp-up areas |
| [04 · How to work with me](personal/04_COLLABORATION_AND_QUIRKS.md) | Communication style, decisions, collaboration, conflict, feedback and fun details |

## Five things that explain me more than a personality test

1. **I follow the dependency chain.** I find it difficult to celebrate a finished screen while the underlying source is unreliable.
2. **I enjoy connecting disciplines.** SQL, statistics, software, automation, data products, interface design and security make more sense together than in separate silos.
3. **I prefer evidence over ceremony.** A failing reproduction and a precise test are more useful to me than a meeting full of untested assumptions.
4. **I like autonomy with responsibility.** Freedom to solve the problem comes with owning documentation, negative tests and consequences.
5. **I build independently because I'm curious.** Projects outside my employment let me explore entire product lifecycles, including things that are messy, incomplete and still worth studying.

The “INTJ” description gives me a vocabulary for preferences such as long-range planning, systems thinking and needing time to understand problems deeply. **It does not measure intelligence, predict technical ability, excuse poor communication or tell anyone how they should work with me.** A personality type is a self-description, not a scientific account of my career.

## My personal motto

**One mind. Every layer.**

It does not mean I should do every job alone. It means I care about the interactions between jobs, and I want to understand a system well enough to work productively with specialists in every layer.

- [Volume I: OmniMaster Handbook](OMNIMASTER_HANDBOOK.md), career and technical autobiography.
- [Volume II: Engineering Field Guide](OMNIMASTER_FIELD_GUIDE.md), diagrams, investigations and worked decisions.

# OMNIMASTER | BUILD A SYSTEM WITH ME
### Volume V · From source events to trustworthy decisions, one verified boundary at a time

**Cayelaem Jantjies | A complete, fictional, runnable engineering walkthrough · November 2026**

[GitHub cover](../README.md) · [Volume I: My engineering history](OMNIMASTER_HANDBOOK.md) · [Volume III: Academy](OMNIMASTER_ACADEMY.md) · [Data-to-Decision code](../projects/data-to-decision-platform/) · [Live interactive Study Room](https://omnimaster-study-room.cabo-solutions-za.workers.dev/)

---

> I don't want someone to leave my GitHub merely thinking I know a lot of tools. I want them to know **how to start with a confusing problem, break it into contracts, build a small system, verify it, find what isn't proven, and explain the decisions to another human**.

This is an applied counterpart to my previous volumes. The code is not a giant platform, but a fully **reproducible synthetic example** spanning data contracts, ingestion, SQLite transactions, current state, metrics and testing. Every chapter explains the choices, alternatives, failure scenarios and limitations.

## Your working project

[**Open the Data-to-Decision Platform source →**](../projects/data-to-decision-platform/)

~~~bash
git clone https://github.com/CayelaemJ/CayelaemJ.git
cd CayelaemJ/projects/data-to-decision-platform
python cli.py demo
python cli.py failure
python -m unittest discover -v
~~~

Only Python 3.12+ is needed. Data is fictional, storage is in-memory, no packages are downloaded and no external service is contacted.

### What you will observe

| Stage | Meaning | Evidence you can inspect |
|---|---|---|
| **Source** | Eight fictional events from two organisations | The `sample_events()` fixture |
| **Boundary** | IDs, source positions, timezone-aware timestamps and nonnegative cents | `validate()` and negative tests |
| **Bronze** | Immutable-style event history with unique identity | `bronze_events` table and replay tests |
| **Silver** | Current version per tenant/account and DELETE tombstones | `silver_accounts` projection |
| **Gold** | Synthetic active-account counts and balances by tenant | Parameterised `metrics_for()` query |
| **Operations** | Atomic failure, duplicate replay and independent reconciliation | `cli.py failure`, `reconciles()` and unit tests |

The sample's expected Gold result is **23,000 cents for fictional-alpha** and **37,000 cents for fictional-beta**. Both groups have two active accounts. The numeric values are *test fixtures*, not real financial data.

~~~mermaid
flowchart LR
    S["Fictional source events"] --> C["Contract validation"]
    C --> B["Bronze event log"]
    B --> P["Silver latest state"]
    P --> G["Gold tenant metrics"]
    B --> R["Independent replay"]
    R --> P
    C -->|"Invalid event"| X["Rollback entire batch"]
~~~

## The six guided chapters

| Chapter | Question | Practical result |
|---|---|---|
| [01 · Define the source](build-with-me/01_SOURCE_AND_CONTRACT.md) | What is an event, and who owns the truth? | Source contract and validation tests |
| [02 · Ingest with guarantees](build-with-me/02_INGESTION_AND_TRANSACTIONS.md) | What must be atomic, unique and replayable? | Transactions, version and duplicate behaviour |
| [03 · Model the current state](build-with-me/03_PROJECTIONS_AND_GRAIN.md) | How do history and latest state differ? | Bronze/Silver/Gold and semantic reconciliation |
| [04 · Deliver the metric](build-with-me/04_FROM_METRICS_TO_USERS.md) | What makes a number useful and appropriately scoped? | Metric contract, privacy boundary and API design exercise |
| [05 · Break and prove the system](build-with-me/05_FAILURE_LAB.md) | What happens when inputs conflict or processing fails? | Failure injection, expected invariants and regression tests |
| [06 · Make the production boundary explicit](build-with-me/06_BEYOND_THE_DEMO.md) | What would be required before real customers used this? | Auth, checkpoints, durable storage, operations and cost roadmap |

## How this project resembles my actual work

It connects habits I developed in enterprise reporting, manufacturing, data platform experiments and full-stack work:

- **BI and manufacturing:** define grain and source truth before computing a measure.
- **Data engineering:** make ingestion, replay, historical changes and error paths explicit.
- **Backend development:** treat database transactions as correctness boundaries.
- **Security-conscious delivery:** distinguish a tenant parameter from actual authorisation.
- **Technical leadership:** write down the rejected alternatives and release evidence.

It does **not** reproduce any employer's code, actual The Fixer architecture or a live CDC service. The point is to teach general reasoning without exposing proprietary systems or overstating a demonstration.

## Two extra routes

**[30-Day Engineering Expedition](THIRTY_DAY_ENGINEERING_EXPEDITION.md)** gives a day-by-day plan to create a real portfolio project, with tangible artifacts rather than an arbitrary course badge.

**[Live Interactive Study Room](https://omnimaster-study-room.cabo-solutions-za.workers.dev/)** runs as a standalone Cloudflare Worker website with scenario questions and optional browser-local progress. [Its HTML source](interactive/index.html) remains public in this repository.

## What you should have when you finish

A clear problem contract, a runnable synthetic dataset, deterministic tests, documented failures, a metric whose grain you can explain, an honest security boundary, a system design decision log, and a list of production capabilities still missing.

**Build small, understand deeply, test the denial path, and learn to say what is *not* verified.**

[Start Chapter 01 →](build-with-me/01_SOURCE_AND_CONTRACT.md)

# THE OMNIMASTER HUMAN INTERFACE
### Volume VI | UI/UX engineering: designing for people, not merely for screens

**Cayelaem Jantjies · A practical account of how I build interfaces, learn from users and connect experience design to data and software engineering.**

[← GitHub profile](../README.md) · [My engineering story](OMNIMASTER_HANDBOOK.md) · [Engineering Academy](OMNIMASTER_ACADEMY.md) · [Interactive Study Room](https://omnimaster-study-room.cabo-solutions-za.workers.dev/)

---

> My work doesn't end when the data is correct. The person on the other end must be able to find it, understand it, trust it and act on it. That is why UI/UX development matters to me.

I have built dashboards, interfaces and application workflows across analytics and independent software projects. Working across SQL, APIs, React, reporting, mobile UI and authentication taught me that **usability is a system property**, not a layer of decoration added to finished code.

This volume explains how my thinking evolved from “make the information visible” to **“make the right action understandable, accessible and recoverable.”** I am involved in UI and UX development as part of my cross-stack work. I do not use that fact to invent a dedicated job title or claim that every usability hypothesis has already been validated with external research participants.

## Read by interest

| You want to know… | Start |
|---|---|
| How I became interested in interfaces beyond analytics | [01 · My UI/UX engineering journey](human-interface/01_MY_UX_JOURNEY.md) |
| What actually matters when people use software | [02 · Designing for real humans](human-interface/02_HUMAN_CENTRED_DESIGN.md) |
| How the ideas connect to products I build | [03 · Case studies and design reasoning](human-interface/03_UX_CASE_STUDIES.md) |
| How I build consistent, inclusive experiences | [04 · Design systems and accessibility](human-interface/04_DESIGN_SYSTEMS_AND_ACCESSIBILITY.md) |
| How I test whether an interface works | [05 · Usability research and measurement](human-interface/05_MEASURE_USABILITY.md) |
| How to practise and follow the same path | [06 · UI/UX workbook](human-interface/06_UX_WORKBOOK.md) |

## What changed my understanding of interface design

A technically correct dashboard can still make someone choose the wrong option. A successful API request can still leave a user wondering whether their change saved. An authentication screen can be secure but impossible to recover from. A visually impressive product can fail on narrow screens or with keyboard navigation.

I started paying attention to the entire journey, not simply the component.

~~~mermaid
flowchart LR
    NEED["Person's goal"] --> UNDERSTAND["Understand their context"]
    UNDERSTAND --> TASK["Design the task flow"]
    TASK --> INTERFACE["Build a usable interface"]
    INTERFACE --> TEST["Observe, test and measure"]
    TEST --> IMPROVE["Repair the friction"]
    IMPROVE --> TASK
~~~

## The seven questions I ask about an interface

1. **Purpose:** what job does the person want done, and how urgent is it?
2. **Clarity:** can they tell what the system is showing and what to do next?
3. **Feedback:** what confirms success, saving, loading, failure or an irreversible action?
4. **Control:** can they undo, retry, correct or safely abandon the operation?
5. **Access:** does it work for different devices, abilities and technology constraints?
6. **Trust:** are data freshness, permissions, AI uncertainty and consequences explained?
7. **Evidence:** did we observe task success, or did we merely like the mock-up?

A UX designer learns the user's mental model. A UI developer makes the design behave predictably. A data engineer makes the state behind it correct. I enjoy the connections between all three.

## My project contexts

- **Enterprise dashboards:** metric labels, filter logic, chart clarity, performance and decision-making.
- **The Fixer:** ingestion setup, source previews, validation errors, role-aware workflows and administrative tools.
- **CABO Learning Hub:** distinct learner, parent and educator journeys, privacy, age-aware patterns and assessment feedback.
- **Mobile and responsive work:** narrow-width controls, readable charts, dark-mode behaviour, focus and platform differences.
- **OmniMaster portfolio and study room:** navigation, discoverability, interactive learning and a directly observable UX mistake: an HTML source link does not launch the experience.

Some of these are active product design or test workstreams, not proof of launched features or formal end-user study results. The chapters distinguish design intent, implementation and verified behaviour.

## The purpose of this volume

I want readers to be able to critique their own apps, not simply copy my colours. Each chapter includes a decision framework, examples and exercises. The workbook asks you to design a task, test it with people where possible, and improve it based on real observations.

**An interface should help a person succeed, not make them admire how hard the developer worked.**

[Start with my UI/UX journey →](human-interface/01_MY_UX_JOURNEY.md)

# THE OMNIMASTER ARCADE
### Learn something, break something safely, and solve it like an engineer

[← GitHub cover](../README.md) · [Academy](OMNIMASTER_ACADEMY.md) · [Personal manual](OMNIMASTER_OPERATING_MANUAL.md) · [Play the terminal game](../projects/omnimaster-incident-academy/)

---

## 01. Incident Academy | The executable game

**Eight cases. Three choices each. Explanations after every decision.**

The game runs entirely offline using Python's standard library, with no personal data, scores uploaded, accounts or API keys.

~~~bash
git clone https://github.com/CayelaemJ/CayelaemJ.git
cd CayelaemJ/projects/omnimaster-incident-academy
python quest.py
~~~

The cases cover duplicated invoices, CDC freshness, cross-tenant access, AI citations, database cutovers, SQL indexing, MFA and release gates.

**[START THE INCIDENT ACADEMY →](../projects/omnimaster-incident-academy/)**

## 02. Choose your own production incident

You are the technical lead for a *fictional* analytics platform. It's Friday afternoon. A dashboard reports **6,000** in revenue while the source invoice shows **1,000**. One order has two deliveries and three inspections.

What's your first move?

<details>
<summary>A. Add a DISTINCT to the amount and send the release email</summary>

**Bad ending: The Mirage.** Two different orders can have the same amount. DISTINCT(amount) may hide duplication while losing legitimate revenue. You corrected a number without correcting its meaning.

**Recovery:** return to the source record, define each fact's grain, check join cardinality and write a reconciliation test. No production patch from this fictional story.

</details>

<details>
<summary>B. Check the join grain, then reconcile the source amount</summary>

**Good ending: The Investigator.** You discover 2 × 3 = 6 joined rows. Each repeats the original invoice value. Separate the invoice-grain measure from delivery and inspection counts, then verify the result remains stable when more inspections arrive.

**Unlocked skill:** trace a KPI defect upstream rather than reformatting the visual.

</details>

<details>
<summary>C. Rebuild the dashboard in an entirely different framework</summary>

**Bad ending: The Expensive Detour.** The wrong SQL can look wrong in any frontend. The root cause moves with the data. You're now debugging a new framework *and* the original accounting error.

**Recovery:** isolate the correct source measure before choosing any new platform.

</details>

## 03. A small gallery of fictional engineering villains

| Villain | Signature move | How to defeat it |
|---|---|---|
| **Count Duplicator** | Turns a one-to-many join into inflated revenue | Declare grain, reconcile counts, test cardinality |
| **The Green Pipeline** | Marks a batch successful without checkpoint progress | Progress invariant, retries, negative tests |
| **Captain Stale Cache** | Serves yesterday's truth with today's timestamp | Freshness SLA, provenance and invalidation |
| **The Privilege Phantom** | Hides a button but leaves the endpoint unguarded | Server-side permission and tenant checks |
| **Citation Phantom** | Invents a source the model never read | Grounded evidence and human review |
| **The Friday Cutover** | Wants to migrate without final sync or rollback | Writer fencing, parity, staged rollout |

They are invented characters. The failure classes are real engineering concerns.

## 04. Mini puzzles you can solve without a terminal

<details>
<summary>SQL puzzle: three sales rows total 120, 120, 80. What happens with SUM(DISTINCT amount)?</summary>

You get **200**, not the correct **320**. DISTINCT(amount) removes a legitimate duplicate value. Uniqueness belongs to the business event ID, not the amount column.

</details>

<details>
<summary>CDC puzzle: why doesn't filtering UPDATED_AT >= last_watermark give perfect event history?</summary>

It helps replay boundary rows but cannot reconstruct multiple changes overwritten in the same current-state record or physical deletes with no retained event. Replayed rows also need idempotent handling. Choose capture semantics that match the actual requirement.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Security puzzle: a React screen refuses a cross-tenant ID, but direct HTTP accepts it. Is the app secure?</summary>

No. Client-side rejection is useful feedback but not an authorisation boundary. The API must verify identity, operation and data scope server-side.

</details>

<details>
<summary>AI puzzle: the assistant claims 99.9% confidence, but its quote is not in the document. Should the answer pass?</summary>

No. Self-reported confidence is not proof. Check approved sources, actual evidence and task-level accuracy. Consequential decisions require human oversight.

</details>

## 05. The XP board (on the honour system)

| Badge | Earn it by doing this | Proof to keep |
|---|---|---|
| **Schema Sleuth** | Explain a grain mismatch and write a test | Before/after totals and query |
| **Replay Ranger** | Show that duplicate events don't duplicate state | Idempotency test |
| **API Gatekeeper** | Deny a cross-tenant request at the backend | Negative HTTP test |
| **Evidence Guardian** | Reject a fabricated AI citation | Input, expected result and test |
| **Rollback Pilot** | Demonstrate a reversible migration in a local environment | Restore/rollback transcript |
| **Documentation Wizard** | Teach someone how to run your system without help | Clean-run README and reviewer notes |

These are **self-study milestones**, not certifications, GitHub achievements or endorsed credentials. Don't make fake commits or issues to collect them.

## 06. Play the multiplayer version

Try this with a friend or study group:

1. **Investigator:** read a fictional defect and identify the invariant.
2. **Sceptic:** challenge the first proposed fix with a counterexample.
3. **Builder:** implement the smallest change in an isolated environment.
4. **Reviewer:** reproduce the negative test and check the documentation.
5. **Teacher:** explain the result in plain language.

Switch roles after each case. Nobody gets to solve a data-grain bug by changing CSS.

## 07. The easter egg: my real “superpowers”

<details>
<summary>Click to reveal the secret identity</summary>

I'm a developer who spent a lot of time making dashboards and slowly discovered that most important bugs live **behind** the dashboard.

I enjoy following those bugs until I understand SQL, backend logic, permissions, infrastructure or the business process well enough to explain what went wrong.

My current weakness: there is always another interesting system to investigate.

My preferred power-up: a smaller scope, a test that reproduces the problem and someone who challenges the assumptions.

</details>

## 08. More levels

[Volume III: Take the seven-module engineering course](OMNIMASTER_ACADEMY.md) · [Volume II: Work through seven technical exercises](field-guide/03_ENGINEERING_WORKBOOK.md) · [Run the four original labs](../projects/README.md) · [The INTJ chapter](personal/01_INTJ_AND_ME.md)

The game is fiction. The habit it teaches is simple:**New challenge:** build the real educational capstone in [Volume V](OMNIMASTER_BUILD_WITH_ME.md), follow the [30-day expedition](THIRTY_DAY_ENGINEERING_EXPEDITION.md), or open the [offline interactive study room](interactive/index.html).

 **question the easy answer, verify the invariant, and leave the system more understandable than you found it.**


For the browser-based experience, [launch the live Study Room](https://omnimaster-study-room.cabo-solutions-za.workers.dev/). Read [Volume VI: The Human Interface](OMNIMASTER_HUMAN_INTERFACE.md) for the usability reasoning behind its design.

# THE 30-DAY ENGINEERING EXPEDITION
### Thirty practical missions to learn systems thinking, data pipelines, applications, AI and release engineering

**Designed by Cayelaem Jantjies as a self-study path; no qualification, paid account or professional experience is implied.**

[Academy](OMNIMASTER_ACADEMY.md) · [Volume V](OMNIMASTER_BUILD_WITH_ME.md) · [Live Study Room](https://omnimaster-study-room.cabo-solutions-za.workers.dev/) · [The person behind the methods](personal/02_WHY_I_THINK_IN_SYSTEMS.md)

---

## The promise

This is not thirty days of motivational quotes. Each day ends with **one inspectable artifact and one test of understanding**. If the exercise takes longer than a day, take longer. Progress is not a race.

Use Python 3.12+, SQLite, Git and a code editor. Later lessons optionally use React/Node.js and containers, but the core path is locally reproducible and uses fictional data.

### The journal template

~~~text
DAY:
Business question:
What I predicted:
Smallest experiment:
Result and evidence:
What failed:
What changed:
What I still cannot claim:
Commit or artifact link:
~~~

## Week 1 | Understand source truth

| Day | Mission | Deliverable | Pass criterion |
|---:|---|---|---|
| **01** | Explain the customer/business problem before picking a tool | One-page problem and audience statement | Another person can explain the intended outcome |
| **02** | Create fictional organisations, accounts and events | Versioned synthetic dataset | No real data, keys documented |
| **03** | State the grain and unique keys of each entity | Source contract table | Each row has one unambiguous meaning |
| **04** | Write first SQL create/insert/select statements | Runnable schema script | Clean setup reproduces expected rows |
| **05** | Create a one-to-many join that duplicates a financial measure | Failing demonstration and corrected query | Expected totals reconcile after correction |
| **06** | Compare inclusive and exclusive date boundaries | Temporal test table | A boundary record appears in the intended period |
| **07** | Turn the week's errors into a regression suite | At least five tests and journal notes | Tests catch deliberate duplicate/invalid input |

**Checkpoint:** you can defend your schema, business grain and metric definition without leaning on a dashboard visual.

Read: [SQL modelling lesson](academy/02_SQL_AND_MODELLING.md) · [Query-plan lab](../projects/sql-query-plans/).

## Week 2 | Engineer reliable movement

| Day | Mission | Deliverable | Pass criterion |
|---:|---|---|---|
| **08** | Define an event ID, source position and operation | Event contract | Create, update and delete represented |
| **09** | Write source validation | Invalid-input cases | Malformed IDs, amounts and timestamps rejected |
| **10** | Store events separately from current state | Bronze + Silver design | Raw evidence retained and current view correct |
| **11** | Implement idempotent replay | Duplicate event test | Same input twice does not double-count |
| **12** | Introduce same-version conflict and stale arrival | Reconciliation note | Conflicts reject; stale events do not overwrite newer state |
| **13** | Make one batch fail on a later bad record | Rollback test | Earlier writes in that batch are not committed |
| **14** | Rebuild current state from an event log | Deterministic comparison | Corrupted projection is detected |

**Checkpoint:** you can explain why a green batch isn't evidence of correct source-change capture and what a real checkpoint must guarantee.

Run: [Data-to-Decision capstone](../projects/data-to-decision-platform/) · [CDC replay lab](../projects/cdc-replay-lab/).

## Week 3 | Deliver a user-facing system

| Day | Mission | Deliverable | Pass criterion |
|---:|---|---|---|
| **15** | Define one useful business metric | Metric contract | Population, grain, time and exclusions specified |
| **16** | Create a curated query | Gold SQL or Python aggregate | Matches reconciled source state |
| **17** | Define API request/response and errors | OpenAPI-style outline or Markdown contract | Clear success, invalid input and denial behaviour |
| **18** | Sketch the permission boundary | Identity/tenant/role diagram | No claim that client-side button hiding is security |
| **19** | Build one small CLI or browser view | Usable display of fictional results | Correct labels and documented freshness |
| **20** | Add accessibility/error/empty states | UI or documented test case | Keyboard and readable failure paths checked |
| **21** | Conduct a skeptical peer/self-review | Written design critique | At least three risks and specific tests captured |

**Checkpoint:** the person using your output knows what the number means, how fresh it is and what they are authorised to do.

Study: [Full-stack lesson](academy/04_BUILD_APPLICATIONS.md) · [Metrics chapter](build-with-me/04_FROM_METRICS_TO_USERS.md).

## Week 4 | Add intelligence and release discipline

| Day | Mission | Deliverable | Pass criterion |
|---:|---|---|---|
| **22** | Find one task where AI could help, and one where it should not decide | AI use-case note | Deterministic and human decision boundaries explicit |
| **23** | Build an offline structured answer validator | Source-ID and quote tests | Fabricated evidence rejected |
| **24** | Create an eight-case evaluation set | Test matrix with expected outcomes | Wrong answers, unknowns and failure cases included |
| **25** | Simulate AI provider timeout or no-response | Controlled fallback | System makes no unsupported consequential decision |
| **26** | Identify three application abuse paths | Threat model | Cross-tenant, input and privilege cases included |
| **27** | Write automated checks for your project | Test command and CI plan | Clean run fails on a deliberately broken invariant |
| **28** | Rehearse backup or state rebuild and define rollback | Recovery document | Restore path and residual risks visible |

**Checkpoint:** you understand the difference between a useful demonstration and a safely operated service.

Study: [Applied AI lesson](academy/05_APPLIED_AI.md) · [Release lesson](academy/06_SECURITY_AND_DELIVERY.md) · [AI evaluation lab](../projects/ai-output-evaluation/).

## Days 29–30 | Publish your own textbook chapter

| Day | Mission | Deliverable | Pass criterion |
|---:|---|---|---|
| **29** | Write your architecture decision record | Context, options, choice, tests, risks and rollback | A reviewer can challenge it without extra meetings |
| **30** | Publish your synthetic capstone and teach someone its limits | README, setup, tests, screenshots if helpful, failure diary | Another person runs it and can explain an invariant |

**Final outcome:** a clear repository showing what you built, why you built it, how it can fail and what you still need to learn.

## The three skill badges you can actually earn

These are **personal study milestones**, not official GitHub badges or professional certifications.

**Source Detective:** you can explain grain, identity, temporal boundaries and double-counting.

**Systems Builder:** you can demonstrate replay, atomic writes, bounded scope and a useful consumer metric.

**Evidence Guardian:** you can show negative tests, clear AI boundaries, release gaps and a reproducible README.

## When you get stuck

Follow the routine I use:

1. Reduce the problem to the smallest failing input.
2. Write expected versus actual behaviour.
3. Test one hypothesis at a time.
4. Read the actual source error and inspect the data.
5. If you don't know a tool, learn that one concept rather than replacing the whole stack.
6. Ask another engineer to challenge the evidence.
7. Record the failure and the change in thinking.

A finished day is one with **an honest result**, not necessarily a green result.

# Hands-on engineering labs

These are **runnable portfolio exercises**, distinct from the larger product repositories and confidential client work. They use only synthetic sample data, Python standard library dependencies and local tests.

| Lab | Demonstrates | Run |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [CDC Replay Lab](cdc-replay-lab/) | Event IDs, replay safety, Bronze/Silver/Gold, delete tombstones, source ordering and atomicity | `cd projects/cdc-replay-lab && python -m unittest discover -v` |
| [Data Quality Contracts](data-quality-contracts/) | Ingestion schema, primary keys, finite decimals, timestamp freshness and machine-readable violations | `cd projects/data-quality-contracts && python -m unittest discover -v` |
| [SQL Query Plans](sql-query-plans/) | Composite indexing, sargable date filtering, SQLite EXPLAIN output and result consistency | `cd projects/sql-query-plans && python -m unittest discover -v` |
| [Offline AI Output Evaluation](ai-output-evaluation/) | Extractive answer evidence, schema checks, review gating and synthetic negative tests | `cd projects/ai-output-evaluation && python -m unittest discover -v` |
| [OmniMaster Incident Academy](omnimaster-incident-academy/) | Eight educational decision scenarios across data, BI, APIs, security, AI and release controls | `cd projects/omnimaster-incident-academy && python -m unittest discover -v` |
| [Data-to-Decision Platform](data-to-decision-platform/) | End-to-end synthetic event ingestion, atomic SQLite projection, tenant metrics, replay and reconciliation | `cd projects/data-to-decision-platform && python -m unittest discover -v` |

The labs do **not** imply production deployment, live connectors, customer data access or security certification. Larger systems, Cloudflare/AWS integrations and AI workloads are documented in the corresponding full project repositories.


## Verification

Each project has an isolated standard-library test suite. The [Engineering Labs workflow](../.github/workflows/engineering-labs-ci.yml) runs all six project suites plus the static browser study-room tests on relevant pull requests and main-branch changes; its actual execution status must be checked in GitHub Actions. This is *not* the deployment or production-security gate for other repositories.


## Learn and play

Start with the [seven-module OmniMaster Academy](../docs/OMNIMASTER_ACADEMY.md), then practise decisions in the [Arcade](../docs/OMNIMASTER_ARCADE.md) or run `python projects/omnimaster-incident-academy/quest.py` from the repository root.


## New end-to-end study path

[**Volume V: Build a System With Me**](../docs/OMNIMASTER_BUILD_WITH_ME.md) uses the complete synthetic Data-to-Decision lab to teach contracts, transactional ingestion, metric grain and failure recovery. Pair it with the [30-Day Engineering Expedition](../docs/THIRTY_DAY_ENGINEERING_EXPEDITION.md) and [offline study room](../docs/interactive/index.html).
